node.title: Local Spring Boot web app on the existing banking-app stack
node.question: Where does swe-prep run and what is it built with - the shape (local web app, desktop app, CLI/TUI), where state lives, and the stack - weighed primarily against time-to-first-keystroke and secondarily against being credible portfolio evidence.
node.decision: A local web app on the stack of the captain's existing Team-7-Banking-Application repo: Spring Boot 3.4.3 on Java 21 with Spring Web, Data JPA, Actuator and Lombok; Postgres rather than SQLite; React + Vite for the front end; Monaco for the code editor. It runs locally and is reached over the existing tailnet, autostarted via a systemd user unit. Hosting is not built now but is protected by three decisions: Postgres from the start, the runner behind an interface, and a user id modeled from day one with exactly one seeded user and no authentication.
node.why: The shape is decided by domain coverage, not friction: grading front-end practice means rendering and asserting in a browser, which a terminal app can never do and a desktop app could only fake by embedding a browser. The friction objection to a web app is answered by autostart on the machine's existing systemd user units, making time-to-first-keystroke one click with no cold start. Reusing the banking app's stack means no learning cost and no stack-selection risk, and a Spring Boot backend is itself portfolio evidence because entry-level Java postings overwhelmingly screen for it. Carrying a user id from the start makes adding auth later roughly a day's work, whereas omitting it makes it a refactor touching every table and query.

rejected.alternative: A CLI/TUI
rejected.why_it_lost: It can never render and assert in a browser, so it cannot hold the front-end practice domain - even though it would genuinely have had the lowest friction for a heavy terminal user.

rejected.alternative: A desktop app
rejected.why_it_lost: It would have to embed a browser to fake front-end grading, adding a second platform for no gain.

rejected.alternative: SQLite
rejected.why_it_lost: Its only real advantage was needing no service, worth little against a Postgres already configured and in use behind JPA, and Postgres removes any database migration if the app is ever hosted.

rejected.alternative: Building authentication now
rejected.why_it_lost: A login screen would sit between the captain and his daily drill, adding friction to the one thing whose purpose is removing it, and the expensive part of auth-later is schema ownership, which the seeded user id already solves.

rejected.alternative: Hosting now
rejected.why_it_lost: The captain does not need hosted access today; Tailscale already reaches this machine from a phone, covering the real cases at zero cost, with the accepted limitation that the PC must be on.

node.soundbite: It runs as a local Spring Boot web app with a React front end, autostarted so opening it is one click, on the same stack as the banking app.

node.title: Two-tier daily session with a small required core
node.question: What one daily session looks like: how long it takes, how many exercises it contains, what happens on a wrong answer or when stuck, what 'done for today' means, whether it is a fixed serving or open-ended, and whether partial completion counts - including how a 40-minute algorithm problem fits a short daily serving.
node.decision: A session has three tiers and only the first is required: a warm-up of ~8 quick recall and recognition reps taking about 4 minutes, which alone completes the day; an optional main exercise of one full problem at roughly 30 minutes; and an open continuation with no cap. The warm-up alone earns the streak, and the session shape is domain-agnostic - nothing in it may assume the content is an algorithm problem.
node.why: The minimum session has to be small enough that it is never skipped, because bad days are the only days that matter - good days were never the problem. The warm-up is not filler: pattern recognition is the highest-value-per-minute training for entry-level interviews, and the main exercises are how recognition converts into execution. Separating the streak (showing up) from the exercises (improving) keeps a single-player streak honest. Calibration with the captain confirmed the warm-up reads as genuinely valuable and four minutes is small enough for a bad day.

rejected.alternative: A session whose required minimum is a full ~40-minute problem
rejected.why_it_lost: A 40-minute minimum is a session you skip when tired, and one skip usually ends the habit.

node.soundbite: One day is done after a four-minute warm-up of about eight quick reps, and the full problem after it is optional.

node.title: Public engine, private problem content
node.question: Can Blind 75 problem statements ship in a public repository, and if not, what is the cheapest lawful source of problem text?
node.decision: Ship the engine publicly and keep all problem content - statements, test data, reference solutions, generators - in the private repo the solutions already go to, loaded by the app via a private submodule or a gitignored local path. The public repo carries the engine, the list of problem titles, and optionally a few original demo statements.
node.why: LeetCode's statement prose is copyrighted expression, while titles, the list, and the algorithmic ideas are free facts under 17 U.S.C. §102(b). The streak decision already sent solutions to a separate private repo, and since the authoring unit is statement + test cases + reference solution + input generator, three of the four were already going private - moving the statement across costs nothing and leaves the public repo with zero protected prose. This is also the fastest path to the first daily session, the map's binding constraint, because no 75-statement authoring project stands between now and drilling.

rejected.alternative: An openly-licensed source of Blind 75 / NeetCode 150 statements
rejected.why_it_lost: None exists and none can: Blind 75 is a curated list of LeetCode's problems, and repos claiming to have it either license only their author's solution code or reproduce LeetCode text with no right to grant.

rejected.alternative: Clean permissive datasets (HumanEval, MBPP, Exercism problem-specifications)
rejected.why_it_lost: They are general or entry-level programming katas rather than interview-algorithm curation, so adopting them would mean abandoning the curated set - useful as a format demo, not as the content pile.

rejected.alternative: Scraped-provenance datasets with permissive wrappers (APPS, CodeContests)
rejected.why_it_lost: A permissive wrapper licence does not cure scraped provenance - a licensor can only license what they own, and these aggregate problems from Codeforces, AtCoder and others under separate terms.

rejected.alternative: Writing fresh original statements now, as a gate
rejected.why_it_lost: Confirmed clean, since describing a known problem in original words with your own examples and generated test data produces a statement you own, but it loses as a gate purely on time - good later work for portfolio polish.

rejected.alternative: Scraping Blind 75 into the app
rejected.why_it_lost: LeetCode's ToS forbids crawling, scraping and spidering outright, independent of the copyright analysis and regardless of whether content lands in a public or private repo - off the table permanently.

node.soundbite: Problem statements go in the private content repo with the solutions, so the public repo ships the engine and the title list with zero protected prose.

node.title: Submission judging model
node.question: What the app checks when a submission is run: pass/fail versus partial credit, what feedback appears on failure, whether time and memory limits are graded, whether approach and style are judged, and whether results are durable.
node.decision: Correctness is strict pass/fail with no partial credit, showing the count of tests passed as information rather than a score. On failure the app reports only how many tests failed; revealing the failing case is an explicit request that is always available, recorded visibly, and never penalised, matching the hint ladder's shape. Each problem carries an authored target complexity; after tests pass the user states their solution's time and space complexity before the target is revealed, and the claim is verified by running the submission at growing input sizes and fitting the runtime curve, with only coarse conclusions and 'measured scaling is consistent with your claim' where measurement is inconclusive. There is no style feedback. Resource limits are reported, not graded, with a generous timeout to catch infinite loops. Every attempt is persisted, recording pass/fail, submissions taken, hint-ladder rungs climbed, reveals, the complexity self-assessment and what measurement said, and abandonment.
node.why: Partial credit would invent a number that means nothing and soften the only honest signal available. Reasoning about your own code without an oracle is the skill a real interview tests, and always handing over the failing case trains the opposite reflex; penalising opt-in help only teaches the user to game themselves. Articulating complexity before seeing the target is itself the interview skill, and a self-report alone would congratulate an O(n^2) solution claiming to be O(n) - the single case most worth catching - while empirical scaling reliably catches polynomial blow-up, the error that actually costs interviews. Style nagging is noise and not what interviews reject people over. Grading on wall-clock would punish JVM warm-up and teach nothing. Thin attempt records would quietly cripple the scheduler, which takes this history as its input. The record also accepts real costs: every problem needs a large-input generator, timing on a normal machine is only usable for order-of-magnitude differences, and the runner needs a second execution mode.

rejected.alternative: Partial credit on correctness
rejected.why_it_lost: It would invent a number that means nothing and soften the only honest signal available.

rejected.alternative: Always handing over the failing case on failure
rejected.why_it_lost: It trains the opposite of reasoning about your own code without an oracle, which is why people grind hundreds of problems and still freeze.

rejected.alternative: Penalising use of the failing-case reveal
rejected.why_it_lost: Penalties on a self-imposed system only teach the user to game themselves.

rejected.alternative: Accepting the complexity self-report on its own
rejected.why_it_lost: Unverified, it would congratulate an O(n^2) solution claiming to be O(n), the single case most worth catching; measurement makes it a prediction scored against evidence rather than an honour-system checkbox.

rejected.alternative: Automated style feedback
rejected.why_it_lost: It is noise and is not what interviews reject people over.

rejected.alternative: Grading time and memory limits
rejected.why_it_lost: Grading on wall-clock would punish JVM warm-up and teach nothing.

node.soundbite: A submission simply passes or fails, help like seeing the failing case is always available but always recorded, and after you pass the app makes you state your complexity and then checks it by measuring how your runtime actually scales.

node.title: Grader/Runner split with language-neutral test-case data
node.question: What an exercise is independent of language and domain, what a test specification looks like, what contract a runner adapter satisfies, and how a submission flows from editor to verdict - without hardcoding Java assumptions or over-abstracting.
node.decision: Split Grader from Runner: a Grader decides pass or fail, a Runner only executes, and both are polymorphic. Exercise is the authored unit with prompt, domain, tags, difficulty, hint ladder, response spec and grading spec; Form (Rep or Challenge) is an attribute, not a separate type; Response covers Choice, ShortAnswer, Program, Query and later Component; Attempt is the durable record and Submission one run within it. Test cases are language-neutral JSON data, with each language adapter supplying the harness and stub from a language-neutral signature; LeetCode's serialisation convention is adopted for trees and linked lists. Complexity measurement is optional metadata via an InputGenerator and ScalingProbe over the same Runner, and every row belonging to a person carries a user id.
node.why: Keeping what the user produces apart from how it is judged stops 'exercise' from secretly meaning 'thing that runs code': a concept question has a Grader and no Runner, and warm-up reps exist in every domain because Form is an attribute. Test cases as data are authored once and run in every language ever added, which the record calls the difference between pluggable languages being real and being aspirational. The accepted constraint is that inputs and outputs must be JSON-representable, which most of Blind 75 satisfies; front end is the one place the JSON model does not extend, stated plainly, and the polymorphic Grader and Runner keep it from being foreclosed. Optional complexity metadata never pollutes the concepts layer because exercises without a generator are simply never checked.

rejected.alternative: The obvious design where Exercise means 'thing that runs code'
rejected.why_it_lost: Concepts and warm-up reps become special cases bolted on the side.

rejected.alternative: Writing test cases as JUnit code
rejected.why_it_lost: Every new language would require re-authoring the entire problem set, making pluggable languages aspirational rather than real.

rejected.alternative: Making Form (Rep vs Challenge) a separate type
rejected.why_it_lost: As an attribute it decides only where an exercise appears in a session, which is what lets warm-up reps exist in every domain instead of being an algorithms-only gimmick.

rejected.alternative: Inventing a serialisation convention for trees and linked lists
rejected.why_it_lost: LeetCode's existing convention is adopted since the captain will be reading their problem statements anyway.

node.soundbite: A Grader decides pass or fail while a Runner only executes, and test cases are language-neutral data authored once, so non-code exercises and new languages both fit without redesign.

node.title: Streak mechanics without invented currency
node.question: What actually generates the pull to open the app tomorrow when the captain is the only user and the author, self-imposed points create no obligation, and Duolingo's social and loss-aversion levers are unavailable?
node.decision: Invented currency is cut entirely - no XP, no hearts, no lives, no leagues. Instead: every solved problem is committed to a private repo with private contributions shown on the profile, so the contribution graph is a true external record; the app shows an honest readiness picture derived from existing attempt records instead of a score; a scheduled notification cue at a chosen time; the streak is displayed as a true count of days practised, not spendable and nothing denominated in it; and a missed day may be repaired by a double session the next day, capped at roughly two per month. Only real artifacts are ever committed, never synthetic practice markers.
node.why: Any number the captain can print himself is a number he stops believing in around week two, and a fake number that goes up is actively misleading about whether he is getting hired. What the design can honestly do is remove every excuse, make the record true rather than invented, and make breaking it cost something real: the contribution graph is external, permanent, and cannot be faked; the readiness figures cost nothing to compute and are all true; habit research says the cue matters more than the motivation; and an all-or-nothing streak that breaks makes people quit outright rather than resume, so a capped repair preserves the asset across one bad evening.

rejected.alternative: Invented currency - XP, hearts, lives, leagues
rejected.why_it_lost: The captain knows the points are invented and can edit the database; a self-printed number stops being believed and a rising fake number misleads about actual hiring readiness.

rejected.alternative: Publishing solutions to a public repo
rejected.why_it_lost: The captain declined it; a public dump of Blind 75 solutions reads as interview grinding rather than building, and it would collide with the licensing question if statements ride along. Nothing that mattered is lost, since the witness function was never about anyone reading the solutions.

rejected.alternative: Financial stakes, Beeminder-style
rejected.why_it_lost: They genuinely work, but wiring up money is real friction, and adding a punishment to an activity already being avoided is more likely to increase the avoidance. Available later if nothing else lands.

rejected.alternative: Telling one person - accountability to an actual human
rejected.why_it_lost: It did not lose on merit; the record calls it the strongest effect in the habit literature, outperforming every in-app mechanic combined. It cannot be built, which is exactly why it is written down rather than adopted as a mechanic.

node.soundbite: The streak sticks because the record is true - real commits a person cannot fake, honest readiness figures, a scheduled cue, and a capped repair for a bad evening - not because of any currency the app could invent.

node.title: Practice scheduler: two schedulers over one shared record
node.question: How the app chooses what the captain practises next: whether one spaced-repetition model can serve both reps and challenges, what signal feeds it, how cold-start and graduation behave, and how the standard intervals survive 40-minute problems.
node.decision: Two schedulers over one shared record. Reps get a standard spaced-repetition due-date queue (SM-2, kept swappable). Challenges get a daily priority score - time since last attempt, how badly the last attempt went, pattern under-coverage - with a hard floor on minimum interval, and the highest scorer takes the slot. Both feed on a single 0-5 quality score collapsed from the per-attempt record (5 clean first-submission pass, 3 passed with hints or failing-case reveal, 1 failed or abandoned). Review debt comes first, new problems second, with a weekly cap on introductions. Nothing is ever deleted - a cleanly passed problem earns months-long intervals, which is retirement, not removal. An 'interview soon' mode re-weights the challenge priority score toward broad recency and drops the minimum-interval floor. Once SQL exercises exist, the daily rep set mixes domains in one queue, with domain as a coverage dimension.
node.why: Spaced repetition assumes reviews are cheap, and that arithmetic breaks for a 30-40 minute challenge: twenty due challenges is a fortnight of work, and a scheduler that generates impossible debt gets ignored within a week. The scarcity is structural - roughly 90 challenge slots in three months against ~75 problems leaves barely room for one pass. Due dates ask what is owed; a priority score asks what is worth it, and only the second survives scarcity. Collapsing the rich per-attempt record into a 0-5 score maps directly onto SM-2 and keeps the scheduler from ossifying around today's exact recorded fields.

rejected.alternative: One spaced-repetition scheduler with due dates for both reps and challenges
rejected.why_it_lost: Due dates on 30-40 minute challenges generate impossible review debt - twenty due challenges is a fortnight of work - and a scheduler that generates impossible debt gets ignored within a week.

rejected.alternative: FSRS for the rep queue
rejected.why_it_lost: Better on paper, but the difference over SM-2 is marginal for one user and ~400 reps; the algorithm is kept swappable instead.

rejected.alternative: Feeding raw per-attempt fields into the algorithms
rejected.why_it_lost: Collapsing to a single 0-5 quality score maps directly onto SM-2 and keeps the scheduler from ossifying around today's exact set of recorded fields.

rejected.alternative: Time taken as a scheduling signal
rejected.why_it_lost: It is noise: interruptions, thinking before typing, and typing fast on a misunderstood problem all corrupt it, so it adds variance without carrying information.

rejected.alternative: Unbounded introduction of new problems
rejected.why_it_lost: The classic Anki failure - review debt piles up and the user quits - and ~75 problems can be burned through in two months, arriving at breadth with no depth.

rejected.alternative: Deleting problems passed cleanly three times
rejected.why_it_lost: A cleanly passed problem earns an interval of months; that is retirement, not removal.

rejected.alternative: A separate app or product for interview preparation
rejected.why_it_lost: 'Interview soon' is a different scoring function, not a different app - a re-weighting of the challenge priority score that is cheap to build.

rejected.alternative: Separate per-domain rep queues once SQL exercises exist
rejected.why_it_lost: The scheduler operates over exercises, and domain is one more coverage dimension alongside topic, not a reason for a second queue.

node.soundbite: Reps go through a normal spaced-repetition due-date queue, and each day the single challenge slot goes to whichever problem a priority score says is the best use of forty minutes.

node.title: Warm-up rep types, grading, and authoring
node.question: What a warm-up rep concretely is in each domain: which rep types exist, how each is answered and graded, where reps come from, and how they relate to the main problem set.
node.decision: Five rep types: pattern identification, complexity of a snippet, fill in the missing line, predict the output, and spot the bug (added to the original sketch). Multiple choice by default; predict-the-output is free text graded by exact match after normalisation. Every rep carries a verified explanation, shown immediately on a wrong answer, one keystroke away otherwise, with asking recorded as a behavioural signal. Nearly every rep is derived from a problem already being authored - five to six reps per problem, so ~75 problems yields roughly 400 LLM-drafted, human-verified reps - making the reference solution the seed and leaving one content pile, not two. Derived reps unlock as problems are attempted; ~75 pattern-ID reps work cold on day one.
node.why: Reps train recognition and discrimination while Challenge exercises own production, a division of labour rather than a compromise. Multiple choice grades exactly where the answer set is finite, and the distractors are the entire value. Deriving reps from the problem set dissolves the second content pile, which is where the project most plausibly dies, and eight reps a day against a ~400-rep pool is comfortably sufficient since repetition is the point under spaced repetition. Spot-the-bug is code review, which is genuinely the job, and coheres with the judging decision to make the captain reason about code without an oracle. Gating derived reps behind attempted problems is not a cold-start problem because pattern identification, the highest-value type, works cold.

rejected.alternative: Executing a typed line to grade fill-in-the-blank
rejected.why_it_lost: A Java compile takes a second or two and eight of those destroys the four-minute session; discrimination is the target anyway.

rejected.alternative: Free-text grading for complexity reps
rejected.why_it_lost: The answer set is finite, so free text would only mean normalising O(n^2) against O(n squared) for no benefit.

rejected.alternative: Showing the explanation by default on a correct answer
rejected.why_it_lost: Re-reading something already known is low-value compared to retrieval, and eight explanations would roughly double the session, attacking the property the whole design protects.

rejected.alternative: Buying a confidence signal by interrupting with a flashcard-style 'how hard was that?' prompt
rejected.why_it_lost: Users learn to click through it; the same signal comes from recording whether the captain asked for the explanation, behaviour that would happen anyway.

rejected.alternative: Authoring reps as a second content pile the size of the problem set
rejected.why_it_lost: Nearly every rep derives from a problem already being authored, so the pile mostly dissolves into the existing authoring unit.

node.soundbite: A warm-up rep is one of five recognition drills - pattern ID, complexity, fill-in-the-blank, predict-the-output, spot-the-bug - graded by multiple choice except predict-the-output, and nearly all of them derive from problems already in the set.
